sentences.text: Acaenasuchus, a name meaning 'spine crocodile,' was a very small, narrow-bodied animal that lived in North America during the Late Triassic.

This creature is characterized by highly developed scutes along its pre-sacral series, which feature thornlike processes running parallel along their posterior sides and are ornamented with ridges and hollows not found in Desmatosuchus.

Medial and lateral wing-like structures extend from the ridges of these pre-sacral scutes, while lateral scutes bear two types of horns: conical horns that curve in multiple directions and blunt horns with less curvature.

Unlike Desmatosuchus, the paramedian scutes of Acaenasuchus lack a 'tongue in groove' articulation with adjacent plates, a feature that contributed to a highly flexible carapace enabling swift and agile movement.
Its teeth have rounded tips and broad denticles similar to those of R. callenderi, and a large boss forms the dorsal surface of the orbit, possibly representing a fused palpebral bone.

Unlike dinosauriforms, the iliac and ischiadic pedicles in Acaenasuchus are not perforated, and the recovered humerus features three bulb-like structures on the humeral head, though the mid-diaphysis is missing.
Long and Murry noted that Acaenasuchus possessed teeth described as 'ornithischian-like' alongside other unique features.
Unlike Desmatosuchus, Acaenasuchus lacked caudal armor and pectoral spikes, suggesting a trade-off between defense and mobility.
The holotype of Acaenasuchus, a left dorsal paramedian scute, was discovered by Charles Lewis Camp in 1930 from the Blue Mesa Member of the Chinle Formation in Arizona.

Robert A. Long and Philip A. Murry established Acaenasuchus as a distinct genus in 1995, naming the species geoffreyi to honor Geoffrey Long for his patience while his father was working in the field.
Besides the holotype, 95 other scutes are likely attributed to Acaenasuchus.

Until 2016, Acaenasuchus was known only from dermal armor, but excavations that year revealed skull, jaw, and backbone bones, including a specimen known as SMU 75403 described in 2020 that includes cranial, vertebral, and appendicular elements along with new variations in the carapace and shield.

Acaenasuchus is considered a terrestrial organism with little evidence suggesting it had semiaquatic capabilities, and researchers hypothesize that it occupied a similar ecological niche to smaller archosaurs of the Late Triassic.

Due to lateral osteoderms on its carapace, Acaenasuchus is classified under the broader clade Aetosauroformes rather than strictly within Aetosauria, though it belongs to the clade Pseudosuchia, which represents the crocodilian line of archosaurs.
A 2020 phylogenetic analysis placed Acaenasuchus as closely related to Revueltosaurus and Euscolosuchus, and Irmis assigned Acaenasuchus to the family Stagonolepididae in 2005.
Acaenasuchus lived approximately 228 to 216.5 million years ago in North America during the Late Triassic.
Fossil evidence places Acaenasuchus in the Norian stage of the Late Triassic, from 227.3 to 205.7 million years ago.

It is debated whether Acaenasuchus is a juvenile Desmatosuchus or a distinct genus, with researchers citing differences in osteoderm characteristics to argue against synonymy, while some suggest features distinguishing Acaenasuchus from Desmatosuchus might represent ontogenetic variation rather than distinct species traits, and Heckert and Lucas argue that the pitting on Acaenasuchus scutes indicates it is a juvenile Desmatosuchus.

Despite debates, most paleontologists currently agree that Acaenasuchus is a valid genus separate from Desmatosuchus, and recent studies suggest Acaenasuchus is not an aetosaur but is closely related to non-aetosaurian taxa like Euscolosuchus and Revueltosaurus.
